Ecuador Imposes Temporary Tariffs on Imported Construction Materials, Industry Faces Rising Costs

QUITO — Ecuador’s construction materials industry is experiencing significant disruption after the government imposed a temporary 25% tariff on imported cement, steel rebar, and related products last week. The measure, announced as part of efforts to support domestic producers, is already impacting major companies, including Holcim Ecuador SA.

The Ministry of Production and Foreign Trade says the tariff, scheduled to remain in effect for at least 90 days, is intended to "level the playing field" for local manufacturers facing an influx of lower-priced imports. However, businesses warn the move is driving up costs and threatening ongoing projects.

“We are concerned about the sudden increase in input prices,” said Carla Muñoz, spokesperson for the Ecuadorian Association of Construction Material Producers. “Companies like Holcim Ecuador SA and many smaller suppliers are now facing substantial additional expenses that were not anticipated in this year’s budgets.”

Industry analysts estimate that the cost of imported cement has risen by as much as 18% since the tariffs took effect, while imported steel products are now up 15%. Several construction sites in Guayaquil and Quito have reportedly slowed operations due to uncertainty over material costs and supply.

Jorge Paredes, a construction economist at the University of San Francisco de Quito, noted, “The measure may help local factories in the short term, but if prices continue to rise, we could see smaller companies unable to absorb the shock, possibly leading to workforce reductions.”

The National Construction Materials Workers Union has urged authorities to reconsider the duration of the tariff, warning of potential layoffs if higher costs persist. “We understand the need to protect national industry, but we cannot ignore the immediate consequences for workers and ongoing projects,” said union leader Pablo Villacís.

As negotiations between industry representatives and government officials continue, the sector remains in a state of uncertainty, with many awaiting further clarification on the tariff’s duration and any potential exemptions.
